extracted.intended_audience: high-school student reporters and school newspaper staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing school-newspaper copy — including society stories, features, follow-ups/rewrites, sports reports, and editorials — aimed at student reporters and editors. Covers what to include in leads, structure, style, and required informational summaries/statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society story lead elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead to an account of a social event may feature: (1) the names of the persons giving the party, (2) the names of the guests of honor, (3) the occasion, (4) the number of guests, (5) the entertainment offered, (6) the decorations, (7) incidents of importance, (8) the place, or (9) the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whichever of these lead elements best serves the interest of readers. The example that follows in the text demonstrates correct application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society story tone & scope
rubrics_metrics.description: In all accounts gush, favoritism, and fawning should be avoided. Only social events of interest to a large number of students should be reported in detail. Small private parties are seldom worth more than a few lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly flattering or biased language; prioritize events with broad student interest; reserve short notices for private/small gatherings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story definition and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A story which has no great news value, but which is made interesting by the reporter’s clever treatment; may seek to instruct or to amuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features appeal more to the emotions than to the intellect; they depend on manner of presentation and can be difficult to write well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story style and leads
rubrics_metrics.description: For feature stories informal leads are most effective. The general style is more nearly that of the short story than that of the news article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a narrative, human-interest approach; avoid rigid inverted-pyramid leads; balance emotional appeal without overdoing the emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story author suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inexperienced reporters should not attempt feature stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features require skill in conveying the right amount of human interest; novices should gain experience on simpler pieces first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up vs. Rewrite — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'follow-up' contains late (new) information not included in the first account; a 'rewrite' merely retells the first story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'follow-up' when adding new facts; use 'rewrite' when retelling; label and angle the piece accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up vs. Rewrite — handling & length
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Rewrites’ should be briefer than the stories from which they are taken, for the freshness of the news has been lessened by previous publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often ask reporters handling rewrites to change the features (play up different points). In a follow-up the new information should be featured. High school papers seldom use rewrites and follow-ups except in exchange columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporting — play-by-play requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Get a play-by-play summary of an athletic contest and write a story for publication on the day following the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect sequential details of key plays, scoring moments, turnovers, and momentum shifts so the next-day story reads accurately and vividly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports game report contents (narrative & box)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete game account includes a quarter-by-quarter (or inning/period) narrative of plays and scoring, identification of stars and key plays, and a statistical summary or box score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative should highlight decisive plays and standout performers; the box/summary should provide concise factual data to back the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports statistical summary items
rubrics_metrics.description: Summaries should include: first downs, passes attempted, passes completed, penalties (number and yards), punts (number and average yardage), and scoring by quarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear numeric totals as in example: First down — East 9; West 4. Passes attempted — East 11; West 32. Passes completed — East 5; West 6. Penalties — East, 4 for a total of 65 yards; West, one for 15 yards. Punts — Fisher of East, 14 for average of 30 yards; Hanley of West, 7 for average of 37 yards; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports lineup/substitutions/officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Include starting lineups, substitutions, and the officials (referee, umpire, head linesman) in the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List players by position for both teams, note substitutions and who replaced whom, and record the officials' names to complete the formal record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials fall into three general classes: the educational, the exhortative, and the commentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational editorials explain facts/circumstances; exhortative editorials marshal arguments to promote a course of action; commentative editorials present opinions on matters that attract attention. In all classes, interpretation of news is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial essentials (writer qualities and preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To write an effective editorial, the student must have an interesting subject about which he has thorough and accurate knowledge. He must possess logic and the ability to bring together diverse data to establish definite impressions. He must have a keen sense of humor and be able to admonish his readers without preaching. Above all he must have a good command of English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough research and wide reading improve editorial quality; combine accurate facts with logical presentation and an engaging tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials must be fact-based; not dictatorial
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial cannot dictate. Dogmatic assertion of opinion not backed up by facts usually antagonizes readers and sways sentiment in the opposite direction. All statements must be supported by convincing data. Facts must be the foundation upon which the superstructure of opinion is built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unsupported dogma; assemble convincing evidence before issuing recommendations or criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial subject selection and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the editorials in the school paper should deal with live topics — topics the students are discussing. Some essays on philosophical or historical subjects may be interspersed but should be brief and lively. The school editorial should not be fault-finding in tone; it should boost school enterprises without nagging and without preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long, windy moralizing sermons. Keep editorials relevant, lively, constructive, and targeted to student interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for writing an editorial
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula: First, state the facts or circumstances with which the editorial is to deal; second, state the opinion which is to be established concerning these facts or circumstances; third, state the reasons for the opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structure yields logical and convincing editorials; variations of order are acceptable when appropriate, but the three elements should be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 1 — 'at' with 'about'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use at with about. An event cannot occur at and about the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: He came at about 3 P.M. Right: He came about 3 P.M. (Or: He came at 3 P.M.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 2 — 'alternative' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative means choice between two things, or one of two things between which choice may be made. There can be no third alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: The third alternative was to run. Right: The third course possible was to run. Wrong: I have three alternatives. Right: Three courses are open to me.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 3 — 'appreciate' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciate means to estimate justly or to value highly. It should never be modified by very much or greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: I appreciate the honor very much. Right: I appreciate the honor; or I am greatly honored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 4 — 'aught' vs 'naught'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse aught and naught. The name of the symbol 0 is naught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: I got a big, black aught in the physics examination. Right: I got a big, black naught in the physics examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 5 — 'of no avail' vs 'to no avail'
rubrics_metrics.description: Of no avail should be used only with some form of the verb to be. Use to no avail with other verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: He worked hard, but of no avail. Right: He worked hard, but to no avail. (His work was of no avail.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 6 — 'badly' misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use badly for a great deal or very much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: I want badly to go. Right: I want very much to go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 7 — use of 'beg' in asking permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Beg, when used in asking permission, takes a noun for an object, never an infinitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: I beg to be excused. I beg to differ with you. Right: I beg permission to be excused. I beg leave to differ with you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 8 — avoid 'local' unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the word local unless it is necessary to make clear the idea advanced. Never use it as a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: He was taken to a local hospital. Right: He was taken to a hospital. (If taken to a hospital in another city, specify that fact.) Wrong: The locals scored in the first quarter. Right: The home team scored in the first quarter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 9 — 'reason' vs 'because' clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Never complete reason with a because clause. The reason is always that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: The reason is because I do not like you. Right: The reason is that I do not like you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction rule 10 — 'various' vs 'several'
rubrics_metrics.description: Various should not be confused with several. Various means changeable, or of different kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: Various members spoke. Right: Several members spoke.
